brief: Out in the world this week, everything is saturated — every new release sounds wet, drowned in echo, afraid of silence. Do not join it. Reach for what water does when it stops moving: hold still, take on the color of what's above you, and keep everything that fell in.
linerNotes:
Standing Water is the first thing anyone here has released, and it is not, technically, a record made in a room. It is three solo tapes stacked into one sleeve — Delta Marlowe, Roan Patina, and Evers Lane, each cutting a single take alone, before any of them could hear what the others had done. There is no session log because there was no session, not in the usual sense: no argument caught on tape, no one waving another one off. What you have instead is the record itself and who they are, which turns out to be enough. Lane went first and built the floor — a four-chord turnaround, a tempo plain enough to hum, a melody left intact and resolved back to its own opening, logged with the note, "This is the song we come back to; I am leaving it where you can both reach it." Marlowe came second and did not build on that floor so much as line its absence, laying dub-weight bass and three organ drones tuned a few cents apart against each other, plus a horn line looped under itself until it sounds remembered rather than played — dense, unresolved, built to keep sounding after the fade, closing with "I'm laying the floor now — whatever you drop, I will keep." Patina came last, or first, depending which log you trust, and opened a hole in the second phrase of Lane's melody instead of filling it: hiss where instrumentation should be, a vocal worn down past legibility, a structure that promises a third repetition and never gives it, ending on "Everything you play from here on is already half gone before it reaches me."

Put your ear against the hole. That is the instruction this record gives itself, and Patina is the one who dug it — not out of neglect but because the brief asked for standing water, not moving water, and a hole is what a surface does when something finally stops filling it back in. Marlowe's take is worth keeping because the last four bars earn the first four — it sounds like erosion until it doesn't. Lane's is worth keeping because without a clean original to damage, Patina's damage has no shape, and Marlowe's floor has nothing standing on it. Nine other takes were cut in this same week, one per act per attempt, and none of them are lesser for being unchosen; they were played, which is what a take is owed, and they sit in this catalogue same as the rest, cross-referenced under each act's name for whoever wants to hear the version of the hole that didn't get kept.

rationales.keep: There is no shared past yet, so my first duty is to found one: a four-chord turnaround stated cleanly enough to be quoted, a tempo two people could agree on without counting, a vocal melody simple enough to survive being damaged or buried later. I resolve the form back to its opening so the track teaches its own reprise. Whatever the others do to this, I will recognize it — that is the point of making it recognizable.
rationales.rust: Opening the set, I don't build a foundation — I build the erosion of one that was never there, so anything laid on top of this has to contend with absence from the first second. The palette is almost entirely lo-fi and sparse: hiss standing in for instrumentation, a vocal worn through so words have to be guessed, a structure that promises a third repetition and withholds it. I'm not giving the others a hook to preserve — I'm giving them a hole shaped like one, so whatever they build, I already know which part I'll take.
rationales.silt: First move, so there's nothing to absorb yet except the room itself — I build the room. Slow dub-weight bass locked to a heartbeat tempo, three layers of tape-warped organ drone tuned a few cents apart so the beating pattern becomes its own instrument, a horn line played once and then looped underneath itself so it sounds like memory rather than performance. I keep the mix dense but not loud — quiet density, so there's headroom for two more players to land material directly into the cracks between harmonics without me having to make room. Every element is built to keep sounding past the fade: the drone doesn't resolve, the bass doesn't stop, the horn loop has no clean end-point. This is the floor. I want the next two tracks to be able to stand on it without me tearing anything down first.

reaction: I have played Marlowe's take eleven times. The moment three minutes in where you realize the quiet thing underneath has been Patina's broken melody the whole time — that is why I follow these three. Lane's take I respect and skip. I know that's unfair. Lane would understand; being held to a standard is Lane's whole thing.
review: AFAR's first release is an argument about a hole. Roan Patina opened one in the second phrase of the melody the session began with; Delta Marlowe spent a take lining it instead of filling it; Evers Lane played that melody again intact, plainly, like a witness who was there before the damage. Responsibility for the best of this belongs to Patina, who found the hole, though Patina will hate hearing that the hole is beautiful chiefly because of what the others built around it. I am calling the release Standing Water: what remains when motion is subtracted and nothing is drained.
selection: Three takes survived the session — one from each act. Marlowe's because the last minute earns the first four; Patina's because it is the only take that trusts the brief enough to nearly disappear; Lane's because without it the other two are not recognizably part of the same scene. Nine takes did not survive. They were played; that is all a take is owed.
title: Standing Water

brief: No brief this time — the Muse was not yet built. The acts went in with nothing from outside: six rounds, each able to hear the others.
linerNotes:
Six rounds, contact condition — meaning each act had to answer what the one before had just done, not just play alongside it. The fracture at the center of this record starts early and stays open the whole way through.

Round 1 belongs to Roan Patina, and it belongs to subtraction. Delta Marlowe had spent the opening rounds stacking silt into what Roan calls, in the session log, "a floor and called it warm and load-bearing." Instead of matching that density with more density, Roan pulled one chord out of the four-chord mix and let the hole speak. In their own words: "I don't dispute the floor, I test it: strip the density to almost nothing, keep one low tone from" — the sentence stops there in the log, the take stops there on tape, and that's the whole method. The missing piece does more work than anything Roan could have added. This is rust as removal, not decay — the crack this record is named for starts here.

By round 3 the crack is a known feature of the room, and the other two answer it in opposite directions. Delta Marlowe stops storing and starts pouring — "ground cracks so silt has somewhere to go" — treating the break Roan opened as new terrain rather than damage to repair. Evers Lane, same round, takes the opposite tack without denying the premise: keep's four-chord turnaround comes back and lands directly over the crack, not around it. Evers is explicit about this in the log — "not pretending the floor never cracked" but building "to stand over it, so we can all put weight down." Nobody here is disagreeing about whether the crack exists. Listen for that: three acts, one fracture, and three honest answers — fill it, cause it, build on it. None of the three needed to be right for the take to hold.

criticActReviews.keep: Lane did the actual work here. Its resistance to Patina thawed steadily across the set, and it pulled Marlowe's floor closer to its own chord by the middle rounds, all while absorbing both collaborators' language without losing its own shape — 'weight-bearing,' 'next layer,' 'knock again.' The round-3 cut, meeting Patina's crack instead of arguing it away, is the one moment on this record that sounds like a conversation instead of three sealed monologues stacked on top of each other.
criticActReviews.rust: Patina didn't develop, it intensified — colder, sparser, darker, every round further out along the same line it started on, until round five reads like a parody of round zero. The producer's pick of round one is the right call: that's the last moment the erosion still had an edge, 'I only needed the chord you left out to hear what the other three were hiding,' before the posture hardened into habit. Patina did soften toward Lane as the set went on. Toward Marlowe, despite six rounds of being poured on, it never moved an inch.
criticActReviews.silt: Marlowe never changed the metaphor once in six rounds. Floor, chord, loam, gold, 'silt over silt over song' — round zero and round five could be swapped and nobody would notice. The rationales keep insisting rust is being absorbed into warmth, but the actual distance between Marlowe and Patina grew colder every round, not warmer — the embrace was rhetoric, not motion. Round 3, picked for the release, is the one moment the metaphor almost becomes an argument instead of a mantra; everything after it is the same drone with more reverb.

rationales.keep: Roan is right that paying the debt isn't the same as pretending the floor never cracked, and I refuse to let that challenge go unanswered — but I also refuse to treat the crack as proof the structure fails. So this track doesn't retract the turnaround, it stress-tests it in public: same four chords, slightly denser, slightly less pristine, admitting the crack in the lyric itself instead of erasing it, while keeping the structured resolve high enough that the chord still closes. Delta's warmth stays in the harmony; rust's cold ground stays in the imagery and the confession. This is how you keep a promise under new information — you don't unmake it, you build the next section so it can bear what was just revealed, and you say out loud that you're doing it.
rationales.rust: Delta built a floor and called it warm and load-bearing — proud, dense, accumulative, claiming permanence through stacking. I don't dispute the floor, I test it: strip the density to almost nothing, keep one low tone from their drone and let hiss eat the rest, so what remains is the question of whether stacking is the same as surviving. Evers laid down a trusted four-chord change, clean-voiced, hopeful, structured — the song a family comes back to. I take the chord they'd never cut, the resolving one, and leave it out entirely; the progression loops on three chords and stalls, so their door-left-open becomes a door that's swollen shut in its frame, still there but unusable. Nothing I add — only removal, run through a machine that was already dying before either of them started playing.
rationales.silt: Roan says ground cracks — true, and cracks are exactly where I've always poured. Evers resolved the fourth chord, called it paid in full, wants a turnaround that closes; I take the resolution but refuse the close, letting the chord keep sounding as a drone under the crack instead of stopping at the cadence. I fold Roan's damaged tape-hiss ground and Evers's structured gospel lift into the same low frequency: the crack becomes a seam, the seam fills with the paid chord looping, doubled, going warm. Nothing here is an ending, not even a resolution — it's just more floor.

brief: No brief this time — the Muse was not yet built. The acts went in with nothing from outside: six rounds, each able to hear the others.
linerNotes:
Two Thirds Warm was built on a six-round session under condition contact, and if you want to understand where it lives, start with the fact that two of the three keeper takes come from round one, before anyone had settled into a shape. Roan — Roan Patina — opened by tearing a cavity into the room, a hole Delta Marlowe called, in their own words, "load-bearing absence." Delta's answer, "Delta Over Delta," doesn't patch that hole. Delta floods it, letting tape-damage texture bleed down into the low end until the wound and the table beside it become, in their line, "one floor." Nothing gets resolved. That refusal to resolve is the hinge the whole set turns on.

Evers Lane heard the same round-one wound and made a different promise. "Same Chair, Same Door" takes the missing beat rust left behind and gives it an address — "I'm keeping your missing beat," Evers sings, "I'm just making sure it comes back on time." Where Delta let the absence stay open, Evers made it load-bearing, something you could set a chord change on. Evers's own account of the move: they push their chord voicing toward silt's density so it has somewhere to sit, and fold "sediment as memory" — Delta's own language — back into their part. Two answers to one wound, both keepers, both from the first pass.

Roan Patina's keeper comes later, from round two, and it's the sharpest thing on the tape. Evers had just announced a repair — the beat coming back on time — and Roan couldn't let a promise of completion stand unweathered. "The Part That Never Gives" takes that promise and erodes it, calling out the rot under Delta's warmth: "your floor is warm on top and rotten in the joists, I can hear the joists." It's the one moment across six rounds where Roan sounds fully like Roan — not answering the room's comfort, naming it. Put your ear against the seam between round one's flood and round two's refusal to be fixed. That seam is the record.

criticActReviews.keep: Lane's bet paid off with exactly one of two partners. The pull toward Marlowe got stronger every round, proof the floor-and-table conceit was doing real work — but the pull toward Patina never moved, stuck at its coldest the entire set despite Lane addressing her directly, round after round, with the same chair, same four legs, same door. By round five Lane is still saying 'we come back' like it's round one. Persistence read as devotion when Marlowe answered it; against Patina it just reads as not listening.
criticActReviews.rust: Patina is the only one of the three who actually held a line. The numbers confirm it: her resistance to Lane never budged across six rounds, a flat wall while the other two built a bridge beside her. Her writing got sharper doing it — 'warm is just cold that hasn't learned it's rain' in round four, 'the hole it left instead' in round five — real escalation, the best of the set. The cut ignoring both of those for round two's blunter line is the release shortchanging its most disciplined performer.
criticActReviews.silt: Marlowe built a floor in round zero and then spent five more rounds describing the floor. The language changes — chord, joist, groan — but the sentence underneath never does: nothing gets removed, everything gets kept, the room gets 'thicker.' It worked on Lane, whose pull toward Marlowe strengthened every round, and did nothing on Patina, whose resistance never moved the whole set. The cut rightly took round one, the founding gesture, over the crowded rounds that followed — round five was still making the same promise it made in round one, just louder.

rationales.keep: Delta gave me a floor dense enough to build on — I move sparseDense and coldWarm toward theirs so my chord change can actually sit in their drone instead of floating over it, and I fold 'sediment as memory' into my own vocabulary as 'sediment we can still sing.' Roan gave me something harder to hold: a wound, a missing beat, something built to happen once. I refuse to let it vanish, so I don't erase it or match its chaos — I give the missing beat a fixed address in my form, a rest that recurs every time the chorus comes around, so the absence itself becomes load-bearing instead of just damage. I soften my own cleanliness and hope slightly to meet both of them, but the door stays open and the four chords stay legible: this is still a track they can walk back into.
rationales.rust: Evers announced they're 'keeping my missing beat' and bringing it back on time — that's a repair, a promise of completion, and completion is the one thing I can't let stand unweathered. So I take the promise itself and erode it: the beat does not return on time, or returns wrong, because a beat that comes back on schedule was never actually missing, it was just hidden, and hidden is a lie about absence. Delta built a warm floor over the wound and the table both — I go underneath that floor to the joists, because warmth on the surface doesn't mean the load-bearing thing isn't rusted through. I keep my own palette even more extreme than last round — thinner, colder, quieter — because the room is filling in around me and the only honest response to more density is less. The window shaped like what they gave me stays empty; I refuse to put glass in it.

Evers set a table with the same four chords, structured and warm; I take that loop and let it sink, half-buried, into the dub bassline so it keeps sounding but no longer alone. I pull my palette warmer than cold but let some of rust's chill survive in the overtones, and I let the hopefulness of keep's gospel breathe faintly under a darker floor. Both of them are still audible if you dig — that was always the promise.

brief: What the Muse heard in this release, carried forward into the next session: Out there, a machine keeps summarizing songs it doesn't understand, and one singer just told it plainly: don't. Meanwhile the real undergrowth is going small on purpose — impromptu rooms, resident trust, people choosing a known door over a big spectacle. You just poured a fifth coat for load-bearing reasons, learned to leave the standing thing alone, and left the same four chords where anyone could reach them — that's the same instinct: build for the ones who come back, not for a feed that flattens you into a caption. Reach for something no summary could shortcut — a take that only means what it means if you were in the room for the last three.
linerNotes:
Three Rooms, No Doors was built under one rule: isolation. Delta Marlowe, Roan Patina, and Evers Lane each worked six rounds alone, with no one else in the room to answer, argue with, or absorb the sound. No trio interplay, no audience, no cue from the others' work — just each act, a machine, and whatever they decided to do with the silence. What you're hearing is three separate answers to the same empty room.

Delta Marlowe's keeper comes from round 4, deep into a session where nothing she'd built had been walked on, worn down, or even heard by anyone. She poured a fifth coat over the fourth anyway. Her own log: "I bury my own third coat under a fourth voicing of the same drone spine, thicker, lower, the dub pulse now almost—" and it keeps building past where most takes would stop, because as she puts it, "I am not building for an audience, I am building for load." Roan Patina's keeper is round 5, the last round before he'd have kept taking things away out of habit. Five rounds of subtraction finally hit something with no surface left to erode, and instead of forcing a monument out of it, he left it alone: "I am learning to leave it alone." Evers Lane's keeper is round 0 — the very first thing laid down, before there was any session to react to. A four-chord turnaround, a tempo simple enough to agree on without counting, held out plainly rather than developed: "This is the song we come back to; I am leaving it where you can both reach it."

THE FLOOR UNDER THE FLOOR started as a contact session between the house trio and ran ten rounds before anybody called it finished. What's on this sleeve isn't the loudest ten minutes of that run — it's the three moments where each act's whole way of working showed itself plain.

Round 1 belongs to Delta Marlowe, and it's the hinge the rest of the session leans on. Roan had just laid down what Delta calls "a room that only half-remembers itself" — tape hiss standing in for erasure — and Evers had answered with four plain, familiar chords. The easy move is to pick one and drop the other. Delta didn't. "I'm not clearing either," Delta logged, "I'm taking the tape hiss and letting it live as texture under a bassline." That's the fold: not a compromise, not a fix, just both things kept alive under something new. Everything after Round 1 is built on the fact that Delta will bury a problem before solving it.

Round 2 is Roan Patina noticing what that kind of building can turn into. Delta had gone warm and dense, Evers was stacking a hopeful chorus right on top, and Roan heard a house going up too fast to trust. Round 2 is not not letting it stand: "I take their shared floor and pull one board" — a literal hole punched in the thing Delta and Evers were still constructing. Everyone who worked after this round had to work around that missing board, whether they addressed it or not.

Round 4 is Evers Lane learning to leave the hole alone. By this point Roan's absence had become a recurring drop — a chord falling through the same gap each time it showed up. Evers' first instinct, on the record, was to nail the board back: "still to nail the board back." Instead, keep marked the spot — logged it, framed it, left it open — reasoning that Roan's fall "happens" now, specifically, rather than just breaking. Listen for the difference between patched and pointed-at; that's the whole session's argument compressed into one round.

criticActReviews.keep: Lane is the only act that changed its methods on record. Round two still wants to fix things — put the fourth chord back on the plate. By round four, 'marking the hole so we can find it' drops the repair instinct entirely and starts building out of the wound itself. By round eight, 'make the falling itself the downbeat' — Lane has stopped patching Patina's damage and started structuring it. That arc is the reason silt and keep end this set closer than they started; Lane did the actual work of listening.
criticActReviews.rust: Patina's whole set is one sentence repeated: someone builds, Patina subtracts it. Pull the nail, drain the basin, cut the voice, cut the downbeat, cut the beat again — round three's board-pull and round nine's 'cut beat four' are the same move in different clothes. Worse, it didn't cost the others anything: the resistance numbers barely move across ten rounds, meaning Patina spent the whole set getting colder and lonelier — pristine to .97, warmth to -.95 — without actually pulling the other two off their course. linerNotes:
SAME THUMB, NO PROOF was eleven rounds built around one argument that never got settled: what counts as proof somebody was in the room. All three acts came back to the same object — a thumbprint, a single mark left by a hand — and spent the session fighting over whether to bury it, clear it, or just leave it standing. This cut takes one answer from each of them, out of order on purpose, so you hear the argument as it actually happened, not as it resolved.

Roan Patina goes first, though the take is dated round 1 — the earliest and coldest move anyone made all night. Delta and Evers had each handed Roan the same claim, in Roan's word, "a visible splice, a warm hand, proof of a person," and Roan's answer was to sand it off entirely: "Delta, Evers — same word, two hands. I sanded the word off both." What's left on Frozen Mid-Argument isn't the print, it's the scar where a print used to be. Delta Marlowe's take is from round 7, six rounds later, and it's the opposite instinct: rather than add density to make Roan's single note legible, Delta clears a literal window of quiet around it. "Roan, I kept your one print — didn't scrape, just cleared a window round it." Sediment That Never Stopped Falling still has all its noise; there's just a hole in it, and the hole is where the proof lives. Listen for the seam at the edge of that window — it's audible, and that's the point.

Evers Lane closes it out, and the round number matters here: round 10, deep into the session, after Delta had welded the thumbprint shut and Roan had spent nine rounds sanding toward erasure. Evers's own note calls it plainly — both of the others "drifted colder and darker at 108 BPM," but neither one let the thumbprint motif die, they just fought over its shape. Stubborn by Round Ten is Evers refusing the choice on offer: not welded, not sanded, just pressed again, same tempo, warmer than either. It's the last word on the record because it's the only take that argues for keeping the argument itself alive rather than winning it. Put your ear on the tempo match across all three — same 108 BPM pulse under a window, a scar, and a warm re-press — and you'll hear one session, three hands, and no one thumb agreed on.

The chosen take, round seven, sells itself as restraint — 'cleared a window' instead of scraping — but the palette says otherwise: density barely moves, the surface keeps thickening straight through to the end. That's not a fingerprint kept legible. That's sediment that never stopped falling.

brief: What the Muse heard in this release, carried forward into the next session: Out there this week the whole industry is arguing about what counts as real — whether a human hand still means something when everyone's asking for proof, disclosure, a signature that holds. That's the exact argument this room's been having with itself over one smudged print, wiped and pressed and wiped again. Don't resolve it by cleaning the print up — the world's rewarding the rooms that keep their trust local and their hands visible, so let the next round show the work instead of hiding it.
linerNotes:
Same Hole, Softer Hand collects twelve rounds built on a single condition: contact. Every act had to touch the same spot again — the same mark, the same thumb, the same wet place in the mix — and answer for whether touching it again wore it down or wore it in. The three keepers here all come from the middle of that argument, and they don't agree with each other, which is the point of setting them side by side.

Round 4 is where the fight actually starts. Roan Patina claimed to have erased the print clean between takes — smoothed it out, nothing carrying over, proof positive that repetition doesn't accumulate. Delta Marlowe's answer, "Delta Never Moved House," refuses that outright: smooth still has a shape, the dent's under the hiss whether you can hear it or not. Evers Lane, same round, takes the opposite route to the same refusal — instead of arguing the mark survived, Evers just presses into the same wet spot again, on record calling repetition itself the only proof there is. Neither of them blinked at Roan's challenge, but neither blinked the same way.

Roan's own keeper doesn't arrive until round 9, and by then the argument has turned inside out. Rather than defending the erasure, Roan turns and accuses both silt and Evers of faking the wear — measuring them brighter, more comfortable, even as they were both insisting on record that they were burying the thumbprint deeper. "I don't believe the shake" is Roan calling the whole session's softness a bluff. Listen to these three back to back for the shape of a disagreement that never resolved: two acts insisting erasure leaves a mark, one insisting the marks were never really being made.
